title: Max and the Day of the Dead Ofrenda
author: Shellfie original
credit: An original story written for the McKinley Bulldogs.

pages: At the end of October, McKinley builds a big ofrenda in the main hallway, near the front office. An ofrenda is an altar for Día de los Muertos, the Day of the Dead. It is a holiday from Mexico, when families remember people they loved who have died.

Every student is invited to bring a photo of someone they want to honor. It can be a family member, or even a favorite author, athlete, or singer. Students write their name and room number on the back, put the photo in an envelope, and turn it in to the front office.
Max thinks for a long time. Then Max chooses a photo of Grandpa, who used to take Max to the park and push the swing higher than anyone else. Max feels a little sad, but also happy remembering him.

When the ofrenda is finished, it is beautiful. There are orange cempasúchil flowers, which are marigolds, with petals that make a path. There is colorful papel picado, which is paper cut into delicate designs. There are candles, sugar skulls called calaveras, and pan de muerto, a sweet bread. Families also add favorite foods of the people being remembered.

Max finds Grandpa's photo between a picture of a famous soccer player and a drawing of a little dog. Max whispers, "Hi, Grandpa." Lupe stands next to Max and squeezes Max's hand. "My abuela is up there too," she says. On Día de los Muertos, nobody is forgotten. They are remembered with flowers, food, stories, and love.
